sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Makemake** ​(*makemake*) — ‌Creator, Fertility, ‌Bird-Man ​· To ​see, to ​know ​— belongs ​to the ‌Polynesian ​tradition, where ​it ‌is catalogued ​under the ‌domain ​"Creator, Fertility, ‌Bird-Man". The ​name ​means "To ​see, to ​know"[^1].

​**Makemake** is ‌the creator ​god ‌of Rapa ​Nui — ‌Easter ​Island: father ‌of ​fertility, lord ‌of the ​seabirds, ​and the ‌hidden face ‌behind ‌the island's ​birdman cult. ​His ‌carved eyes ​watch from ​the ‌stone village ​of Orongo, ​where ‌each spring ​a ‌contest chose ​the tangata ​manu, ​the man ​who bore ‌the ‌god's sign ​for a ‌year.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ​the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Makemake** ‌and serves ‌its ​temple at ‌[its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/makemake/). The ​displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ​computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*makemake* ​contains the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in modern ​Polynesian ​orthographies; macron ​usage ​follows ​each tradition’s ‌reference ​dictionaries. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"To ‌see, to ​know"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ​**Makemake** matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*makemake* contains ‌the ​same letters, ‌so ​no lost ‌diacritics ​or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ‌The ‌editorial work ​is ​to ‌fix one ​reviewed ​reference spelling, ‌preserve ​capitalization and ​provenance, ‌and keep ​the ‌original evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ‌a ​description computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ‌**m** ​→ **M** ‌— ​Same, capitalized
- ​**a** ​→ **a** ‌— ​Same
- ​**k** → ​**k** ‌— Same
- ​**e** ​→ **e** ​— ‌Same
- **m** ​→ ‌**m** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **a** ​→ ‌**a** — ‌Same
- ​**k** ​→ **k** ​— ​Same
- **e** ‌→ ‌**e** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/makemake/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**makemake** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Makemake.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Makemake" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Makemake" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"makemake" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Makemake ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Makemake ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Makemake ‌place ​creator, fertility, ​bird-man ​at the ​center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Makemake ‌appears in ​polynesian ‌tradition ​as creator, ​fertility, ​bird-man. The ​name's ​meaning, ‌"To see, ​to ‌know", ​shapes the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ​(Cult)

Devotees ‌and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ​Makemake ​in ‌ritual, text, ​and ​iconography, ensuring ‌the ​name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ‌record.

​The ​myths of ​Makemake ​survive in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, ​and later ‌retellings. ​Each ​version reflects ‌the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ​— poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex entry ​does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Makemake ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Makemake ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Makemake, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​creator ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Makemake ​is the ‌god of ‌the ​watching face: ​on an ​island ​of 165 ​square kilometers, ‌where ​every horizon ​ends in ‌ocean, ​creation was ‌a matter ​of ‌sight — ​the god ​who ​sees, the ​god who ​knows. ‌His cult ​turned that ‌metaphysics ​into sport: ‌each year ​the ‌whole society ​wagered its ‌fertility ​on who ​could first ‌see, ‌and bring ‌back, a ​single ​egg. The ‌birdman contest ​is ​among the ‌most beautiful ​institutions ​in the ‌ethnographic record ​— an ‌election ​without ballots, ​a kingship ​without ​war, legitimacy ‌conferred by ‌a ​seabird's arithmetic. ‌And the ​lesson ​of the ‌silence matters ‌as ‌much as ‌the contest: ​traditions ‌recorded from ​the last ​elders, ​like the ‌chants Métraux ​wrote ​down in ​1934, are ‌not ​museum pieces ​but threads ​— ‌cut, they ​take whole ‌cosmologies ​with them. ‌Makemake's staring ​eyes ‌at Orongo ‌are a ​reminder ​that being ​watched is ​the ‌oldest form ‌of being ​known.[^1]
